div.head: CHARACTERS
div.p: English: Original French:
* This character and the soldiers may be omitted in production.
Five men, two women

div.head: Scene: Dr. Peacock's house.
div.p: Flem Truly, Dr. Peacock, you're a clever man. I've been a pharmacist for twenty-five years and never met a doctor who practiced medicine like you.

Peacock Indeed, no other doctor of my acquaintance has penetrated nature as deeply as I have. But I don't like to praise myself; I can't stand flattery. I want you to come home with me to discuss an important matter. Now, has any one asked for me while I was away? TRIPPET, hey, TRIPPET!

lg.l: How you do scream! Well, sir, what can I do for you?
Has Lady Bellaston asked for me?
So much the better. It's a sign her medication is working. How about

div.p: Peacock Good. It's to tell me that the purge I gave him yesterday has cured him of his pleurisy.

Trippet The poor man died during the night. His son came to tell you. He was in a fury and cursed you and Mr. Flem. I took your part and he cussed me out, too. Happily, I can deal with that. I listened to him very calmly.
Peacock What right has he to complain? I gave him the best treatment. I bled him more than twenty times and purged him frequently. He ought to be cured according to the books.

lg.l: And died according to bell and candle.
Get out of here, impudence. Leave criticizing doctors to the surgeons.

div.p: (Exit Trippet.)
Flem Between you and me, Dr. Peacock, I don't have a high opinion of that purge.

lg.l: It worked effectively most of the time—excepting the Judge.
Also, excepting your wife who you buried last year.

div.p: Peacock Not at all. A good doctor pursues his calling without any regard to a bad result. Otherwise, teaching in medical school might be called into question and where would we be then?

lg.l: I never deviate from established practice.
Well now, let's talk of the business I brought you here for. You know
I've always regarded you as my best friend.

div.p: Flem You are right to do so. I have been a friend of your family for many years. It was I who furnished the drugs during your father's last illness.
Peacock I thank you for it. Ever since I've written my prescriptions only for you.
Peacock Moreover, I've had you get rid of inexpensive, useless drugs. And whenever I write a prescription, I never forget to write it for five or six grains more than the patient needs.

lg.l: And I always put in seven or eight grains less than you prescribe.
That way I save the life of the patient and your reputation.

div.p: Peacock Consider the way we work together. I prescribe imaginary medicines found only in your apothecary shop. I praise their healthfulness, their propriety, and your skill in blending drugs.
Flem And for my part, I never miss a chance to praise you. I speak of your miraculous cures—which, in truth, I've seen very few of.
Flem And, I tell all the patients who come to me about you, praise you to the skies, and belittle or disparage all other doctors without exception.

Peacock We do everything that a doctor and a pharmacist can do for each other. We work in perfect harmony. And, to further our friendship, I am going to tell you about a little investment I have made. I've taken out a ten thousand pound Tontine on him.

lg.l: You know what a Tontine is, of course?

div.p: Flem Certainly, a Tontine is—a Tontine is—(helplessly) What the devil is a Tontine?
Peacock (smugly triumphant) It's a last man out club. The survivor gets all the money from all the policies.

lg.l: That's clever. So if you die—
The policy's not on my life—but on that of a peasant of sixty who
you wouldn't take to be forty. He's the father of one of my servants.

div.p: Peacock I've taken out this policy on him and he's agreed to make me a beneficiary in return for free medical care.

lg.l: A fellow like that, in my hands, will become immortal.
Suppose that he only lives, say one hundred years.

div.p: Peacock Isn't it certain, that in fifteen or twenty years, he'll be the only person in his group?
Peacock Five years later, he'll be the only one. Therefore, I'll receive all the money for twenty years.

lg.l: The reasoning is clear. You've put your money to good use.
I'm delighted you approve my project. And you are a beneficiary, too.
Because, I mean to marry you to my daughter.

div.p: Peacock No compliments. And, for the dowry, I'm going to give you half the immense revenue from this insurance policy which you cannot fail to collect. And no, I'm going to show you our gold mine. You'll have to agree he's an excellent specimen.
(Exit Peacock into his house.)
Flem What a man Doctor Peacock is! Some people think he's a little crazy; but what's just happened would go a long way to disabuse them.
(Peacock returns from the house leading Dudley, a sturdy old peasant.)

lg.l: Have a look at this young fellah! Ever see a better built body?
What do you say to those eyes?
How do you find his skin tone?
Open your mouth. (to Flem) Look at those teeth. Perfect condition.
He hasn't even got a cavity.
Like thunder! Constitution of an ox.
He's got all the signs of long life.
Broad and strong. You've made quite a bargain, Doctor.
We're going to get rich, Mr. Flem.
This peasant is a kind of Peruvian gold mine.

div.p: Peacock. Answer my questions, Dudley. When you went to bed last night, did it take you a long time to get to sleep?

lg.l: Soon as my head hits the pillow—poof—I was asleep.
And I wake up at dawn.
And wakes with a ravenous appetite that I have difficulty to control.
Oh, as to that, Doctor, you keep me well regulated.

div.p: Peacock How he roars! This roaring is no good for him. It comes from too many vessels in contact with the diaphragm. To remedy this defect we ought to give him a purge.
Peacock Preceded by a tonic composed of softening laxatives to prevent dry stools. Go quickly, Mr. Flem, and prepare some suppositories and bring them back here.
(Exit Flem.)
Peacock As soon as you possibly can. This business is serious and requires diligence.
Dudley Can't you leave me without tormenting me, Doctor? For the last three days, ever since I put myself in your hands, you've already purged me twice. I want to have lunch and enjoy it.

Peacock Blood isn't necessary to preserve life. I know what I'm doing. I am more interested in keeping you alive than you yourself. Listen, my friend, as soon as I have bled you, I'll cook up a delicious lunch.

lg.l: I want to give you something appetizing. What do you like to eat?

div.p: Peacock Bah! What bad spirit put such a detestable thought in your head? It's too fatty and it clogs your bowels.

lg.l: I seem to have heard that apothecaries like jelloes.

div.p: Peacock True. But, between you and me, they only sell them. They actually prefer stuffed dates.

lg.l: Really—well, how about a nice roast beef?
Too likely to have trichinosis. Dirty.

div.p: Dudley Too dirty, too sweet, too hard, too fatty. What the devil do you want me to eat?

lg.l: With two or three glasses of laxatives.

div.p: (Enter Trippet.)

lg.l: Sir, there's a man down there who insists on speaking to you.
Let's see what he wants of us.

div.p: (Exit Peacock.)

lg.l: You sigh! What caused you to sigh like that, my poor Dudley?
They're going to bleed me again and give me an enema.

div.p: Dudley They say I have extended diaphragm muscles, and I don't know how many other maladies. Yet, I don't feel a bit sick.

lg.l: That's terrible, my friend, that's terrible. Not to know what's wrong.

div.p: Dudley Since I've been in this house, I've lost more blood than I did in twenty years as a soldier.
Dudley Doctor Peacock intends to make me the last survivor of my group—but if this keeps up, I won't last another month.
Dudley Let's speak openly. Even if I survive the bleeding, I won't survive the diet. I'll starve.

lg.l: He practices austerity in his own eating habits.

div.p: Dudley Aie! How can I resist him. He thinks I'm weak and prescribes for my maladies. He watches my food. He forbids me wine. Damn his medicine and science. It would be better not to interfere with nature.
Trippet To forbid wine to a man of your type is the same as forbidding women to a man of a different sort.

lg.l: Trippet, my dear Trippet, are you capable of pity?
Without a doubt. What can I do for you?

div.p: Dudley You run the house. If you would give me a bottle of wine, I will owe you my life.
Trippet Heaven preserve me from doing such a thing. If the doctor has forbidden you wine then that proves it isn't good for you.

lg.l: I beg you, on my knees.
At least give me a pork chop.

div.p: Dudley Ah, if only I were young again. You'd give me the keys to the wine cellar.

Peacock (entering and seeing Dudley on his knees to Trippet) Ah, Dudley! How passionate you are! My God! That's no way to prepare for an enema. Come along, return to your room and try to calm yourself while waiting for the return of Mr. Flem. (Dudley leaves) That's funny, really.

lg.l: Do you have any idea what he wanted from me?
It's not really difficult to figure out. Dirty old gallows-bird.

div.p: Trippet He was trying to cajole me with his sweet talk and passionate gestures—but I'm not that kind of woman.

lg.l: Good, Trippet. Don't give in to human weakness.
I'd let him croak before he could have any.

div.p: Peacock Now wait a minute—if he shows any signs of croaking! You must satisfy him, Trippet! Ahem! I intend that he live a long life.

Peacock Oh, that! Trippet, they've come to get me to see a patient—a feverish cantor who refuses to drink a purge—but before I leave, it will be easier if I talk to my daughter. Tell her to come see me. (Exit Trippet) I suppose I could find a better husband for Harriet than this Flem. For example, a bureaucrat or a down-and-out gentleman. But I prefer to pay off my own debts, not someone else's. Instead of which, I will exploit my daughter for all she is worth.
Peacock Something you will like. I've decided to marry you. I've chosen a man for you who is extremely knowledgeable and will give you complete satisfaction.

lg.l: Now we're headed in different directions.

div.p: Peacock Listen! What's all this about, if you please? I haven't even told you his name—only of his worthiness, and you are making faces, both of you.

lg.l: It's not his worth that displeases—it's his incompatible qualities.
Eh! Yes, sir. Those qualities are certainly found in an old dotard.
You are painting a wretched portrait of a handsome young man.
But, I don't propose to marry my daughter to some old fuddy-duddy.
Yes, Mr. Flem. He's only fifty. Not old enough to be too virtuous.

div.p: Trippet A virtuous man is not for Miss Harriet, and I am going to prove it. In order to know the worth of a virtuous husband, is it not necessary for the wife to be dispirited herself? First, give her a young man of twenty, and not only will she be fine, she'll have a reasonable husband.

Peacock Nice reasoning. A smart daughter ought not to examine her future husband too closely. She ought to consider it a pleasure to find one agreeable to her father. Understand, Harriet? Now, on my return, I expect to find you disposed to receive the hand of Mr. Flem. (exit)
Harriet Did you hear, Trippet? Is there a misfortune equal to mine? Isn't it enough to lose hope of being with Worthy? Now, I must reconcile myself to becoming the wife of this detestable Mr. Flem.
Harriet Worthy, dear Worthy, what will your despair be when you hear this news?
Trippet Alas! I believe I can already see how unhappy he will be. What a lively sadness moistens his eye. What tears mix with yours. Oh, I loathe the old apothecary.

Trippet I'm not joking. I don't know any more than you what the future will hold. But my point of view is different. You see despair and I see cause for hope. I read the future in a way that is more agreeable than you do.

Harriet You are deceiving yourself. I am already unhappy enough to be married to Mr. Flem. Without doubt, I will gag of it. But I will fulfill my destiny. The more I have to suffer, the more my character will grow.
Trippet I know very well that character thrives on hardship—but sometimes hardship corrupts a pure heart.

lg.l: I hear a noise. Someone is coming.
It's he, himself, Trippet, and your loveable Jeremy.

div.p: Trippet You come just in time, gentlemen. Help us avoid the storm that threatens us. Dr. Peacock has promised his daughter to Mr. Flem.
Jeremy To that flat-nosed pharmacist with thick glasses who works in his shop?

lg.l: So true that the marriage may take place at any time.

div.p: Worthy Oh, Harriet! How can you let them drag you to the altar without making the least effort in my behalf?

lg.l: What do you expect me to do, Mr. Worthy?

div.p: Jeremy Ladies, you have only to follow us to our inn. Our horses are all saddled. We will disappear with you both.

lg.l: Good idea. We'll disappear. All's fair in love and war.

div.p: Worthy Jeremy, I beg you. Think up some plan to prevent this detestable marriage.

lg.l: That's what I'm dreaming up. Use your imagination, too, Trippet.
You're good at this sort of thing.
All right. Let's stir up our imagination.
Well. What have you come up with?
Dammit, I can't wait forever. I've already decided on the best plan.
Simply to make Flem and Doctor Peacock quarrel. Won't that do it?
Right, eh? See how easily I solve the most difficult puzzles.
But, you haven't said how we'll do it.

div.p: Jeremy Right. How to do it? Listen, hasn't some rich person recently died at their hands?

Jeremy That's our luck! All we have to do is to tell the Doctor that Flem says it was the Doctor's prescription that killed the patient. At the same time, we tell Mr. Flem that the Doctor is blaming everything on the way the prescription was compounded.

Trippet I tell you, it won't work. Mr. Flem and Dr. Peacock are too hand-in- glove. For twenty years they've been killing people—some of the nicest people in this city—and they never quarrel over it. And you think they're going to quarrel over a mere magistrate. Why, they've done in lords and ladies.

lg.l: I've got another idea. This one is matchless. Is it true that Doctor
Peacock has an insurance policy on some peasant?

div.p: Jeremy So much the better. This gives me the plan, which I believe, must infallibly succeed. I would like to speak to this peasant.

lg.l: There's the door to his room. You can go in. He's alone.
Leave it to me. That's all I need to know.

div.p: (Exit Jeremy.)

lg.l: What do you suppose he's up to?
I don't know, but Jeremy is a world-class trickster.
I've got an idea of my own. See if we don't slow this marriage down.
You bring me back to life.

div.p: Harriet You don't know how much I'll owe you if you save me from this odious husband.

lg.l: Time will tell if you mean that.

div.p: Trippet Poor children. It would be a terrible shame to separate you. You only want to be together.
Jeremy (returning, and still speaking to Dudley) Yes, you have only to do as I told you and you will be delivered from the Doctor's tyranny. Until we meet again. Adieu.

lg.l: What? You've already talked to Dudley?

div.p: Jeremy I only had two words to say to him. I've warned him. If he plays his role and all goes well, Miss Harriet will today change her name to Worthy. And, as for you, Trippet, I permit you to think of possessing me.

lg.l: How do you intend to work these miracles?

div.p: Jeremy I'm going to disguise myself as a Colonel. Worthy will be my Major. And, as Dr. Peacock doesn't know us because we've always been careful never to come here except when he's visiting patients—ah, what a trick I will play on him. I intend to consult him on a pretended illness. (low to Trippet) Well, Trippet, you're good at this sort of thing. What do you say to it?

lg.l: I approve of it. That's all I have to say about it.

div.p: Jeremy I will instruct you as we go. Let's leave now. Time is precious. I'm going to prepare everything. (to Harriet) No goodbyes, beautiful lady. (to Trippet) See you soon, you little flirt. You, Major, follow me.
(Exit Jeremy and Worthy.)

lg.l: Do you think it will work?
Don't let me languish any more. Listen to me.

div.p: Trippet Hush! Our lovers were right to leave. Here comes Mr. Flem. Follow my lead and pretend to be delighted to marry him.

lg.l: Don't complain. He can easily be fooled.

div.p: (Enter Flem.)
Trippet Ah, ah! Mr. Flem, we've heard news of you. You want to marry my mistress?
Flem It's the Doctor who's taken it into his head that I shall marry. As for myself, I never thought of Miss Harriet because of the difference in our ages.
Trippet What difference! You're joking, Mr. Flem. Do you know, you look as young as a man of twenty-five.

lg.l: Well, as to that matter, I'm still juicy. Got a lot of sap left in me.
You're cute. You have regular features, good color, noble bearing,
graceful manners, and as for your figure, let Miss Harriet speak. (to
His hypodermic syringe is just ravishing.
It suits him better than a sword.

div.p: Trippet And the most gallant cummerbund doesn't look better than his work apron.

lg.l: Behold a tasty, well-turned-out dish of a man.

div.p: Flem It's delightful to me to hear such words from your mouth, dear lady. They distill an amorous syrup in my soul. Yes, my dear, I already sense the birth in my heart of a feeling for you that I had for my late wife. Haven't I told you, doll, how we lived together, my wife and I?

lg.l: Ours will be just such a perfect union.

div.p: Trippet Tell us about if, if you please, sir. I'm just crazy to hear about happy marriages. They're so unheard of.

lg.l: Madame Flem had a lively affection for me.

div.p: Flem On my side, I had a particular care for her health. I didn't wait till she was sick to give her a remedy. Every day, by way of precaution, I made her take some medicine.
Flem When she was the least bit sick, I redoubled my efforts. Alas, the poor woman didn't live long.
Flem She had a very delicate constitution. But, if she died, if was not for want of medication. Not for want of remedies.
Flem To give her a breath of life, I didn't spare a single drug in my apothecary.

lg.l: He's worthy of all the feeling I have for him.
No, sir. I swear, I'm not flattering you at all.

div.p: Flem For you, sweetheart, I promise to take the same care and the same attention, I lavished on my first wife.

lg.l: Every morning and night I will give you some little delight.

div.p: Flem Goodbye, beautiful star. I have to leave you to find Dudley. How impatient I am to have you joined to me. When I even think of it, I am happy.

lg.l: You love the pleasures of imagination.
Yes, but I like physical ones better.

div.p: (Exit Flem into Dudley's room.)

lg.l: What a man, Trippet. I hate him more than I love Mr. Worthy.
You hate him so much already?
Rather than marry him, I am capable of going to the last extremities.

div.p: Trippet Stay of that mind. It may be helpful if we can't manage things in an honest way.

lg.l: Shut up, you fool, my father is coming.
Well! Trippet, in what frame of mind is your mistress?

div.p: Trippet In a mood to obey you. Oh, indeed, we've had a change of mind since you left. We paid attention to your wise advice. Do you know, sir, that we've learned to love old men?
Trippet Ask Mr. Flem in what manner we received him. Presently, we have eyes only for your old friend.
Peacock I don't know if you're speaking seriously, but the fact of the matter is, an older man is better.
Trippet A thousand times better. I wish someone would give me the choice between an old man and a young musketeer. It wouldn't take me long to make up my mind, let me tell you.

lg.l: In fact, an old boy tends to be very indulgent towards a young wife.

div.p: Trippet Oh, yes. In place of a young man who is indulgent only towards his friends. An old husband leaves us his wealth by dying and a young one doesn't die until he's gobbled up our dowry.
Peacock Sometimes that girl is pretty smart. Now, Harriet, I'm delighted you no longer dislike Mr. Flem—

lg.l: What did she say under her breath about dying?
She says she'd rather die than lose him. She's crazy about him.
Well, that's a passion that's arrived rather suddenly.
But, it's a sort of madness, Trippet.

div.p: Trippet Assuredly. Now, if you were to forbid her to love him, she would love him even more.

lg.l: Who are these people coming here?

div.p: (Enter Jeremy and Worthy.)

lg.l: They seem to be some kind of soldiers.

div.p: Jeremy (disguised as a colonel) I am looking for Dr. Peacock. They say he looks rather large and bloated. Necessarily, it must be you.
Jeremy Ah, sir, let me embrace you. In the fashionable world you are often spoken of. They say you are a clever doctor and your prescriptions are written in elegant Latin.

lg.l: Ah, ha! Who are these lovely ladies?
This is my daughter and this is her maid.

div.p: Jeremy To show you how much honor I feel for you and everything that belongs to you, I insist on embracing them, too.

lg.l: Do you take us to be barmaids?
Have you more than one daughter?

div.p: Jeremy So much the worse. When they are made like these they can be easily married off.
Peacock Well, God willing, I'm just about to marry her to an apothecary friend of mine.
Jeremy Very good idea. Your patients certainly won't have to wait for enemas and purges.

lg.l: The more I look at your daughter, the more I find she looks like you.

div.p: Jeremy Word of a soldier! She's you in miniature. Your eyes are the same except for the coloring. Her little nose becomes large like yours: oval face, square face; really the resemblances are astonishing in certain families.

lg.l: Come, sir, if you will. What are you getting at?

div.p: Jeremy That maid of yours is making eyes at me. Apparently, I was made to be the sport of a wench. They always tease me.

lg.l: Sir, for God's sake, tell me who you are.

div.p: Jeremy I am a colonel and you see me here with my major. I come to consult you about an illness.

lg.l: Why are you running off, pretty ladies?

div.p: Trippet We don't want to hear the conversation of an officer who consults a doctor.
(Exit Trippet and Harriet.)
Jeremy I want to tell you, sir—no boasting—I'm well thought of by the combat troops.

lg.l: I'm sure of it, and I congratulate you, sir.

div.p: Jeremy When there's something particularly tough to do, they always call for me. Ask my major.

lg.l: So, you see, I have all the honor and reputation I could wish.
Unfortunately, my body isn't made of iron.
I came down with asthma in Germany while I was pursuing the enemy.
The cause of your illness is worthy of—

div.p: Jeremy Here's how it happened to me. I reconnoitred an enemy scouting party. I attacked them; they resisted. I redoubled my efforts. They regrouped. Then, they fled. I followed them, but then I was obliged to give up the pursuit. I couldn't get my breath. They said I have swollen glands. So, since then, I've been asthmatic.
Peacock (aside) He's consulting me for his own amusement—but I will mock him in his turn. (aloud) You wish a remedy that will soothe you?

lg.l: I have an infallible remedy. But, I have a scruple about curing you.
I think you should keep your asthma and seek a disability pension.

div.p: (Enter Dudley from the house and Flem after him.)
Jeremy What do I see? There's a face I've seen before. Yes, my word, it really is! It's Rosebud. Major, don't you recognize him?

lg.l: It's Rosebud all right. The deserter.
Oh, yes, sir, it's me. I beg for pardon.
Coward! Fortune has delivered you to justice.
Oh, Colonel, have pity on me.
Say, what! God! Why did you disappear without leave?
The Captain was always beating me and there was nothing I could do!

div.p: Jeremy For God's sake, abandon the battlefield because you were beaten? To avenge yourself on your captain, couldn't you wait till after the battle? Major, call Sergeant Slaughter and some soldiers to take this deserter to the guardhouse.
(Exit Worthy to the street.)

lg.l: You never told me, you bastard, that you were a deserter.
I never dared to tell you, sir.
What a mess this wretch has got me in.

div.p: (Worthy returns with several soldiers.)

lg.l: Sir, I beg you to pardon him.

div.p: Jeremy (folding his arms) It upsets me, gentlemen, not to be able to do as you wish. But, when it comes to punishing infractions of military rules, I am inexorable.

lg.l: I should look to my pension.
I'll furnish you all the medicine you need for your old age.

div.p: Jeremy (after a struggle) No. No. (to soldiers) Hurry up, take this clown without more discussion. You will see that this poor devil will die as quickly in my hands as in yours.
(Enter Trippet and Harriet.)

lg.l: What noise is this I hear? What brouhaha are you making here?
Intercede for me, Trippet. They want to hang me as a deserter.

div.p: Trippet Why, gentlemen, if you want to kill him, why not leave him in the hands of Dr. Peacock?

lg.l: Grant him his life, Mr. Colonel.
Don't pester me any more. Guards! Seize him!
It's easy to see what the outcome will be with these people. (aloud)
Listen, Mr. Colonel, so as not to waste time talking, I am going to
count out a hundred gold pieces—or more.

div.p: Trippet What, sir, can you resist the sound of money and the prayers of a beautiful lady?

lg.l: How can I resist? I am not a judge. Do you take me for a judge?

div.p: Trippet Dr. Peacock has a ten thousand pound insurance policy on the life of this man.

lg.l: That's right. Would you consider going shares on him?
I don't know what to do.
If you wish to kill him, let us die with him.
Well, then—let him run the gauntlet.
Listen, Mr. Colonel, I've got an idea how to fix everything.

div.p: Jeremy What, me! For God's sake, my dear friend, if you don't have a better idea than that, Rosebud is going to hang.

lg.l: Oh, it's too much. Colonel. You've go to give it up. Free him.
That's easy for you to say. But, if you were in my place—the rank of
Colonel would cause you to speak differently.

div.p: Jeremy All right! You marry her and I consent at that price to spare the deserter.

lg.l: Come no, Mr. Major, consider how charming she is.

div.p: Worthy I have little taste for marriage—but to please the Colonel—I'll do it. But, only if the doctor gives me a large dowry. It is not right to marry a woman who brings nothing.
Jeremy He's right, Doctor. It's necessary to make it worth his while. Make over all your wealth to him.
Peacock Your humble servant. I prefer you to hang Mr. Rosebud. I'll be off much cheaper.

Trippet Mr. Major, you seem generous. Accept my mistress on the same terms she was to be married to Mr. Flem. That's to say, for one-half the interest on the ten thousand pounds that the Doctor has put on the head of Dudley.

lg.l: To accommodate you, sir, I would like to consent.
And, I won't object. I free you of your promise, Doctor.

div.p: (Exit Flem.)

lg.l: But, who will care for me? The father-in-law or the son-in-law?
I will. I will treat you as I always have.
That being the case, I prefer to run the gauntlet.
No, Rosebud, no. I will care for you. I will care for his health.

div.p: Jeremy I've suddenly taken it into my head to get married, too. With this flirt.
Peacock What, Colonel? You wish to marry the maid after having refused the mistress?
Jeremy I will ennoble her. There, Trippet. From wench, I make you a lady of quality.

lg.l: It won't be the first such metamorphosis.

div.head: CURTAIN
div.p: TRANSLATOR'S NOTE: A few lines of dialogue have been added to the play explaining what a tontine is. Tontines were named for an Italian Banker named Tonti who discovered the scheme. Strange as it may seem this play got Le Sage in a great deal of trouble because the government was employing the Tontine as a means of raising revenue and this play was regarded as a subversive attack on the revenue system of the monarchy.
